item.title: APOD: 2026 November 2 – A Long Cloud on Mars
item.description:
Discover the cosmos!Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation:What’s causing this unusually long cloud onMars? Known as theArsia Mons Elongated Cloud(AMEC) and first recorded by NASA’sViking Orbiter 2in 1977, thestrange cloudhas been imaged in greater detail more recently byESA’s roboticMars Expressspacecraft. Thefeaturedimageis from 2018. Thecloud formsonly duringspringand summerseasonsand then only during morning hours. Made of water-ice, the most familiar process that causescloud crystalstoform around bits of dustwould fail due to the thinness and lack of dust high in theMartian atmosphere.Leading speculationholds that dust is not involved. After the cloud forms near the volcanoArsia Mons, wind blows the clouddownstream— creating a tail that can extend over 1500 kilometers. Efforts to better understandAMECs will continue, an understanding that may bolster amore complete viewofcloud formationonEarth.Tomorrow's picture:eyeing a cat

item.title: Pennsylvania’s Grand Canyon
item.description:
Amid the warm hues of fall foliage, Pine Creek Gorge forms a deep scar in the Allegheny Plateau.
North-central Pennsylvania is canyon country with an Appalachian flair. Pine Creek Gorge reaches depths of about1,500 feet(460 meters) along its gently curving path through the forests of theAllegheny Plateau. Instead of thesteep rock wallscharacteristic of canyons in the desert Southwest, lushly vegetated slopes outline the dramatic topography. In autumn, greens give way to a palette of reds and goldssought outby leaf peepers.
Nicknamed the “Grand Canyon of Pennsylvania,” the gorge runs for some 45 miles (72 kilometers) from Ansonia south to Pine Creek’s confluence with the West Branch Susquehanna River, reaching its greatest depths around Waterville. TheOLI(Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGSLandsat 8satellite captured this image of Pine Creek Gorge on October 25, 2026, when colorful fall foliage was on display.
Glaciers played a key role in the canyon’s formation, though ice itself did not carve it. Pine Creek onceflowed to the north, opposite of what it does today. As glaciers advanced into the region from the northeast during the last ice age, they dammed the river and filled the valley with lakes. Those lakes eventually overflowed, sending water streaming to the south.
When the ice receded, Pine Creek was already becoming entrenched in its southward course. Rocks and sand left behind by the melting ice further prevented the water from turning back north. Glacial meltwater continued to rush through the valley, deepening and shaping it into its current form.
Today, the hillsides around the gorge are blanketed innorthern hardwoodand mixed oak forest, sprinkled with hemlock and white pine. In autumn, the deciduous trees impartred and gold huesto the landscape akin to the rock of the famousArizona canyon.
This seasonal change around Pine Creek Gorge has not always been so visually pleasing. With increasing demand for wood products in early 19th-century America, loggers found their way to the area’s stately trees. At the time, white pine and hemlockseveral feet in diameterand towering hardwoods populated the slopes around Pine Creek Gorge. The pines were especially valued for making ship masts, and hemlock bark was used to tan leather. Before railroads, logs were floated down Pine Creek to the Susquehanna in massive drives. By the early 20th century, decades of logging left the land so barren that the area earned the moniker “Pennsylvania Desert.”
The forest has since returned, and with it,wild inhabitantssuch as black bears, coyotes, bobcats, timber rattlesnakes, and a diversity of songbirds. In 1968, an area of 30,000 acres (12,000 hectares) was designated aNational Natural Landmark. Visitors can experience the gorge’s natural splendor at many points along its path, including from multiple state parks and thePine Creek Rail Trail.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from theU.S. Geological Survey.Photo byfishhawk, via Flickr. Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 1 – Colors of the Moon
item.description:
Discover the cosmos!Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation:What color is the Moon? It depends on the night -- and the time. Outside of theEarth's atmosphere, thedark Moon, which shines by reflected sunlight, appears amagnificently brown-tinged gray. Thefeatured imagehighlights a collection of apparent colors of the full moon on Earth, documented by one astrophotographer over 10 years fromdifferent locationsacrossItaly. Ared- oryellow-colored moon usually indicates a moon seennear the horizon. There, some of the blue light has been scattered away by a long path through theEarth's atmosphere, sometimes laden with fine dust. Ablue-colored moonis more rare and can indicate an atmosphere carrying largerdust particles. What created the purple moon isunclear-- it may be a combination of several effects. The last image captures the totallunar eclipseof 2018 July -- where the moon, inEarth's shadow, appeared a faint red -- due to lightrefractedthrough air around the Earth.Have youever seen an unusually colorful Moon?Tomorrow's picture:open space

item.title: APOD: 2026 October 31 – Night on a Spooky Planet
item.description:
Discover the cosmos!Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation:What spooky planet is this?Planet Earth on a dark and stormy night, of course. The ghostly scene wasphotographed at Hverir, a geothermally active area found along northeastern Iceland'svolcanic landscape. Triggered bysolar activity,geomagnetic stormshave unleashed energetic particles trapped in Earth's magnetic field. Penetrating the planet's upper atmosphere at high latitudes, the particles createauroral displaysin the starry night sky. Ghostly towers of steam and gas are venting fromlocal fumaroles to danceagainst the eerie, greenish northern lights. For now, auroral activity on planet Earth remains in a high state as the Sun is only in early phases of decline from the peak of itssolar activity cycle. And soon, other ghostly apparitions may dance in your neighborhood.Happy Halloween!Tomorrow's picture:many moons

item.title: NASA Releases MAX POWER Key Events for Media, Participants
item.description:
America’s newest aerospace expo and air show – MAX POWER – is fast approaching, and NASA has announced key events beginning Friday, Nov. 6, and running through Sunday, Nov. 8, hosted on and near the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
Through multiple park experiences atMAX POWER, NASA and a variety of external collaborators will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space. NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase Moon rovers, spacecraft, and more. The expo also is a culmination of the agency’s recentInspiration Tour, which included numerous flyovers to highlight NASA’s fleet of aircraft.
A current schedule of events is available on the agency’swebsite.
MAX POWER includes opportunities to meet leadership, astronauts, engineers, scientists, and other subject matter experts during the family-friendly public events with gates opening at 9 a.m. EST on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8.
NASA also will share multiple news updates during the weekend, including hosting a news conference at 5 p.m. on Nov. 7, to provide its latest Moon Base update. Located near the lunar South Pole, theMoon Baseis humanity’s first outpost for long-term lunar exploration.
Live coverage of the news conference will stream on a variety of platforms online. Learn where to watch:
Media credentialing for this event is closed. Media approved for this event must request interviews in advance. Space in the news conference is limited, and first come, first served. Media also may participate in the news conference virtually. To request call details or an interview, please contact Lauren Low in the NASA Headquarters newsroom at:lauren.e.low@nasa.gov.

item.title: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope Captures Eerie Cat’s Head
item.description:
Intricate structures within theCat’s Head Nebulaare illuminated in this mid-infrared view from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope released on Oct. 29, 2026. The distinctive “cat’s head” shape of the nebula was likely sculpted over time by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars in the Carina Nebula. As this stellar feedback erodes the surrounding gas and dust, denser material within the feline-shaped pillar resists erosion, at least for now.
Image credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)

item.title: NASA Explores Potential Commercial Servicing for Hubble Telescope
item.description:
NASA issued a Request for Information Oct. 29 to learn more about industry capabilities for in-space servicing to support the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope.“Hubble still has important science ahead of it, and we should be looking at every reasonable opportunity to keep it delivering for as long as possible,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “If there are innovative and cost-effective ways to extend the life of an asset already on orbit, we owe it to the American taxpayer and the scientific community to explore them. Extending Hubble’s life would mean more discoveries, more science, and more opportunities to expand our understanding of the universe.”The Request for Information seeks commercial interest in: potentially conducting a mission to boost Hubble to a higher altitude to extend its science lifetime; servicing Hubble to enhance its capabilities; or performing a safe, controlled re-entry into Earth’s atmosphere or orbital disposal at the end of Hubble’s mission.“Hubble is a national icon that has fundamentally changed how humanity views our universe for more than 35 years,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Commercial industry has rapidly evolved in recent years to offer new capabilities for in-space satellite capture and servicing. Given the time we have until Hubble’s anticipated re-entry, we are eager to explore the breadth of possibilities to boost Hubble to a higher orbit while we develop the flagship mission to follow.”The Request for Information isavailable onlineand will remain open for responses until 3 p.m. EST, Monday, Nov. 30.Like all spacecraft in low Earth orbit, Hubble’s altitude is slowly decreasing over time because of atmospheric drag. Hubble does not have a propulsion system to maintain its own orbit, and analysis predicts Hubble is likely to re-enter the atmosphere in the 2033 to 2034 timeframe. As such, NASA anticipates that a mission would need to take place by 2032.The Hubble Space Telescope has been operating for more than three decades and continues to make ground-breaking discoveries that shape our fundamental understanding of the universe. Hubble is a project of international cooperation between NASA and ESA (European Space Agency). NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, manages the telescope and mission operations. Lockheed Martin Space, based in Denver, also supports mission operations at Goddard. The Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, which is operated by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy, conducts Hubble science operations for NASA.To learn more about NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope, visit:

item.title: November’s Night Sky Notes: Light-Day Away
item.description:
In 1977, NASA launched twin spacecraft Voyager 1 and 2, taking advantage of a once-every-175-year planetary alignment of the four largest planets in our solar system: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Using six gravity assists between them, thisGrand Tourgave us up-close views of the gas and ice giants, including several moons. By the 1980s, the two probes went their separate ways at Saturn. As Voyager 2 continued toward Uranus and Neptune, Voyager 1 grabbed one moreportrait of the solar system(excluding Mercury and Mars), including a final image of thepale blue dotwe call home.
“Hello from the children of planet Earth.”
Every good road trip needs some music to match. In this case, each craft carries theGolden Record, a 12-inch phonograph record with spoken greetings in 55 languages, 27 musical tracks, 116 images, and other sounds from Earth. Each record is protected by anouter coverfeaturing etchings showing our Sun's location relative to 14 pulsars, along with instructions on how to play it. The design used various metals to protect the information encoded from space radiation: the record used copper and gold plating, and the cover used aluminum. The cover was electroplated with an ultra-pure sample of the isotope uranium-238. Uranium-238 has a half-life of 4.468 billion years.
Did you know that a light-minute is a measure of distance, not time? In August 2012 and November 2018, Voyager 1 and 2 crossed the heliopause, the boundary where the Sun’s solar wind meets the interstellar medium. Using NASA’sDeep Space Network, Earth communicates with both spacecraft and tracks each on its journey. At the time of this article, the Canberra antenna tracked Voyager 1 at 25.80 billion km, or just over 16 billion miles.
On November 18, 2026, 49 years after its launch, Voyager 1 will cross the one-light-day mark, 16.1 billion miles from the Sun. You may have heard the termlight-yearin your favorite sci-fi movie or show, or when stargazing and referring to an object outside of our solar system.This videobest demonstrates the different distances between the inner solar system, outer solar system, and beyond, using light measurements. Additionally, track each Voyager spacecrafthere.
You can get a real understanding of what a gravity assist might be like with ourGravity Assistactivity and learn what it’s like to measure a “light minute” with ourMeasuring a Kid Minuteactivity guide!

item.title: APOD: 2026 October 30 – Haunting the Cepheus Flare
item.description:
Discover the cosmos!Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.
Explanation:Spookyshapes seem to haunt this dusty expanse, drifting through the night in the royal constellationCepheus. Of course,the shapesare cosmic dust clouds visible in dimly reflected starlight. Far fromyour own neighborhood, they lurk above the plane of the Milky Way at the edge of theCepheus Flaremolecular cloud complex some 1,200 light-years away. Over 2 light-years across and brighter than most of the other ghostly apparitions, vdB 141 or Sh2-136 is also known as theGhost Nebula. It lies at lower right in the starry field of view. Inside the Ghost Nebula are reddish telltale signs of dense cores collapsing in the early stagesof star formation. With the eerie hue of interstellar dust reflecting bluish light from hot young stars ofNGC 7023, the Iris Nebulastands out against the dark just left of center.In the broad telescopic frame, these fertile interstellar dust fields stretch almost six full moons across the sky.Tomorrow's picture:night on a spooky planet

item.title: Vega Island Frozen in Fright
item.description:
The sight of an icy skull-like visage on the Antarctic island could make one’s blood run cold.
Shrouded in ice in the lonely Weddell Sea, Vega Island is an eerie sight to behold. On this speck of land east of the Antarctic Peninsula, ice, rock outcrops, and glacial moraines combine to create the appearance of a smirking skull in profile looking toward Devil Island.
These images show Vega Island’s creepy countenance at the start of austral autumn (left) and in spring (right). They were acquired with theOLI(Operational Land Imager) onLandsat 9on March 22, 2025, and October 10, 2026, respectively. (Clouds obscured the island in March 2026.) Anunatakjutting out of the ice has the appearance of an eye socket, alateral moraineforms a mouth, andBahía del Diablo(Devil’s Bay) Glacier constitutes a jawbone. In the March 2025 image, a layer of snow coats the ice, which is typical of the region’s wettest month. That contrasts with the October 2026 image, when snow is absent from large areas and darker ice surfaces are visible.
Above-averagetemperatures in winter 2026—particularlyin June—were partly responsible for so muchbare ice in October, said glaciologist Mauri Pelto of Nichols College. The ice exposed on Vega and nearby islands indicates limited new snow accumulation over the winter, further reduced by sublimation and wind scouring, he said. “The winter season was no treat for these glaciers.”
The melt season ahead may also be more trick than treat. Bare ice is darker than snow and absorbs more solar energy, meaning that melting is poised to speed up as the days grow longer and warmer. “Even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would be helpful in the short run,” Pelto said. “When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket.”
The first comprehensive mapping of Vega Island’s ice was aided by Landsat imagery. In astudy published in 1982, scientists described the island’s four ice caps with protruding rocky cliffs and outlet glaciers. They leveraged early Landsat observations along with aerial photos and topographic maps to catalog 29 glaciers on Vega.
Of those glaciers, Devil’s Bay Glacier has beenclosely monitoredsince the austral summer of 1998-1999, with researchers measuring anoverall declinein its mass. Satellite images acquired inrecent decadesshow ice loss from other glaciers on the island as well, with increased areas of exposed bedrock.
Long before scientists began tracking its glaciers, Vega was a bright spot in a tale of terror born out of early exploration of the area. TheSwedish Antarctic Expeditionof 1901-1903 set out to study the geography, geology, climate, and wildlife on and around the eastern Antarctic Peninsula. The party became split into three groups during their explorations, isolated for a winter in different locations. Adding to the horror, theylost their shipto the pack ice. Cape Well-met, as it would come to be known, off the “forehead” of the Vega Island skull, was the site of a happy reunion of two of the groups in spring 1903. Soon thereafter, an Argentinean expedition rescued the survivors of the ordeal.
NASA Earth Observatory images by Lauren Dauphin, using Landsat data from theU.S. Geological Survey.Story by Lindsey Doermann.
